transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herbst.
Investigators in Israel think that the co-pilot,
who attacked the captain of a plane flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv mid-air last week,
likely acted alone.
That's according to a person familiar with the matter but not authorized to speak publicly.
NPR's Kat Lonsdorf has more.
The Israeli investigation into the attack is pointing toward the likelihood
that the co-pilot was a lone wolf attacker, that source told NPR.
Investigators in the United Arab Emirates,
which is leading the inquiry working with Israeli officials,
announced they have deemed the incident an attempted terrorist attack,
although the motive is still unknown.
The co-pilot is from Oman, according to Israeli officials,
raising questions about how he was allowed to fly a plane heading to Israel,
as Israel does not allow pilots from countries it doesn't have diplomatic relations with
to fly in its airspace.
Several lawmakers in Israel are demanding an investigation into security failures
that could have led to the incident.
Kat Lonsdorf, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
The midterm elections are just weeks away,
when voters will decide which party will control Congress.
Right now, Republicans control both chambers.
And as political ads flood your social media and your phones,
polls are also being conducted,
some showing Democrats are making headway and that Republicans should be nervous.
And Pierce Domenico Montanaro says midterm elections are always tough on the President's party,
and that President Trump has acknowledged that.
Democrats are the favorites right now to take back control of the House at the very least.
And the Senate, which was considered a long shot at the beginning of this cycle,
seems to be within reach for Democrats now.
But there's a question of how big these gains are likely to be,
because redistricting has really insulated Republicans to an extent.
The Democratic Party isn't very popular either.
There just aren't that many competitive seats.
Less than 10 percent of the House really is competitive.
NPR's Domenico Montanaro, rather, reporting.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has chosen the person who will lead the investigation
into two failed executions this year.
For member station WPLN, Mariana Baca-Yau reports,
Lee is again tapping former U.S. Attorney Ed Stanton.
Lee called for the third party review
after last week's botched execution left Christa Pike in critical condition
but alive at a local hospital.
The current lethal injection process was developed after Stanton's last review
found problems with how the state inspected the drugs it uses to carry out the death penalty.
Lee says Stanton's investigation will determine if the current protocol was followed
and evaluate its effectiveness from there.
In the meantime, the governor has called off the remaining executions scheduled for this year.
For NPR News, I'm Mariana Baca-Yau in Nashville.
President Trump is tapping his director of national intelligence, Jake Clayton,
to head a new government task force on A.I. that Trump's calling the Super Intelligence Force.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Voters in Latin America's largest democracy go to the polls today
in the latest test for leftists in the region,
which has seen a large shift to the right in recent years.
Brazil's incumbent left-wing president is locked in a tight contest with the son of his rival,
the former far-right president convicted of staging a coup, as NPR's Carrie Khan reports.
Both say the contest is too close to call between veteran leftists Luisa Nacional-Lula da Silva
and Flavio Bolsonaro, a current senator.
Lula, now 80, is facing a tough re-election
with voters concerned about crime, corruption, and a faltering economy.
Bolsonaro says if he wins, he will align more closely
with President Trump's anti-drug interventionist policies in the region.
While Trump has not publicly endorsed Bolsonaro,
he says he's watching the contest closely and touts his clout in the region,
which has seen the last seven presidential contests shift to right-wing leaders that align with the U.S.
Lula says he's willing to work with Trump as partners, but insists on respect for sovereignty.
Carrie Khan, NPR News, Rio de Janeiro.
Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz is in Kyiv today,
supporting President Zelensky as Russia intensifies attacks on Ukraine.
Russia is now using hard-to-intercept ballistic missiles and drones
while Ukraine targets Russia's oil industry.
On social media, Merz says Germany's security depends on the war's outcome,
and Zelensky says the two countries will make "important agreements" during today's visit.
I'm Janine Herbst, NPR News, in Washington.

topics.text: Israeli investigators believe co-pilot who attacked plane captain acted alone in attempted terrorist attack
Democrats favored to take back House control in midterm elections, Senate within reach
Tennessee Governor Lee appoints former U.S. Attorney Stanton to investigate two failed executions
President Trump appoints Jake Clayton to head new government task force on artificial intelligence
Brazil's leftist incumbent Lula faces tight reelection contest against right-wing senator Bolsonaro
Germany's Chancellor Merz visits Kyiv to support President Zelensky as Russia intensifies attacks
